claim: Extracellular field potentials (EFPs) are an important source of information in neuroscience.
source: Extracellular field potentials (EFPs) are an important source of information in neuroscience, but their physiological basis is in many cases still a matter of debate.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of EFPs in neuroscience, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: The physiological basis of EFPs is in many cases still a matter of debate.
source: Extracellular field potentials (EFPs) are an important source of information in neuroscience, but their physiological basis is in many cases still a matter of debate.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of scientific understanding about EFPs.

claim: Axonal sources are typically discounted in modeling and data analysis because their contributions are assumed to be negligible.
source: Axonal sources are typically discounted in modeling and data analysis because their contributions are assumed to be negligible.
evidence: This describes the current practice in the field, based on established knowledge.

claim: Contributions of axons to EFPs can be significant.
source: Here, we established experimentally and theoretically that contributions of axons to EFPs can be significant.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by both experimental data and theoretical modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: EFPs are prominent in the presence of terminal zones where axons branch and terminate in close succession.
source: Modeling action potentials propagating along axons, we showed that EFPs were prominent in the presence of terminal zones where axons branch and terminate in close succession, as found in many brain regions.
evidence: This is supported by modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Terminal zones where axons branch and terminate in close succession are found in many brain regions.
source: Modeling action potentials propagating along axons, we showed that EFPs were prominent in the presence of terminal zones where axons branch and terminate in close succession, as found in many brain regions.
evidence: This is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Models predicted a dipolar far field for axonal terminal zones.
source: Our models predicted a dipolar far field and a polarity reversal at the center of the terminal zone.
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical models presented in the manuscript.

claim: Models predicted a polarity reversal at the center of the terminal zone.
source: Our models predicted a dipolar far field and a polarity reversal at the center of the terminal zone.
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical models presented in the manuscript.

claim: Model predictions were confirmed using EFPs from the barn owl auditory brainstem recorded in nucleus laminaris using a multielectrode array.
source: We confirmed these predictions using EFPs from the barn owl auditory brainstem where we recorded in nucleus laminaris using a multielectrode array.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from barn owl recordings.

claim: Axonal terminal zones can produce EFPs with considerable amplitude and spatial reach.
source: These results demonstrate that axonal terminal zones can produce EFPs with considerable amplitude and spatial reach.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from both modeling and experimental results.

claim: Types of EFPs include invasively recorded signals such as the electrocorticogram (ECoG) and the local field potential (LFP).
source: Types of EFPs include invasively recorded signals such as the electrocorticogram (ECoG) and the local field potential (LFP), as well as the noninvasively recorded electroencephalogram (EEG) and the auditory brainstem response (ABR) (Brette and Destexhe, 2012; Nunez and Srinivasan, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Types of EFPs include noninvasively recorded electroencephalogram (EEG) and the auditory brainstem response (ABR).
source: Types of EFPs include invasively recorded signals such as the electrocorticogram (ECoG) and the local field potential (LFP), as well as the noninvasively recorded electroencephalogram (EEG) and the auditory brainstem response (ABR) (Brette and Destexhe, 2012; Nunez and Srinivasan, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: EFPs in the brain were long thought to be primarily of synaptic origin.
source: EFPs in the brain were long thought to be primarily of synaptic origin (Buzsáki et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes historical scientific understanding, supported by citation.

claim: Many modeling studies focused on the extracellular fields induced by postsynaptic currents on the dendrites and the soma of a neuron.
source: As a consequence, many modeling studies focussed on the extracellular fields induced by postsynaptic currents on the dendrites and the soma of a neuron (Holt and Koch, 1999; Einevoll et al., 2013; Lindén et al., 2011; Lindén et al., 2010; Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: Active, non-synaptic membrane currents can contribute to far reaching potentials detectable at the scalp.
source: However, a number of recent data analyses and modeling efforts have revealed that active, non-synaptic membrane currents can play an important role in generating population-level EFPs (Reimann et al., 2013; Anastassiou et al., 2015; Schomburg et al., 2012; Ray and Maunsell, 2011; Belluscio et al., 2012; Waldert et al., 2013; Ness et al., 2016; Scheffer-Teixeira et al., 2013; Reichinnek et al., 2010; Sinha and Narayanan, 2015; Taxidis et al., 2015), including far reaching potentials detectable at the scalp (Baker et al., 2011; Teleńczuk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Currents from the axon are still thought to be so small as to be of minor importance for the EFP.
source: Currents from the axon are still thought to be so small as to be of minor importance for the EFP.
evidence: This describes the prevailing view in the field.

claim: The far field of an action potential traveling along an idealized straight and long axon is quadrupolar.
source: One of the reasons for the assumption that axonal currents contribute little to the EFP is that the far field of an action potential traveling along an idealized straight and long axon is quadrupolar, meaning that it decays faster with distance than synaptic sources, which are typically dipolar (Nunez and Srinivasan, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Quadrupolar fields decay faster with distance than dipolar fields.
source: One of the reasons for the assumption that axonal currents contribute little to the EFP is that the far field of an action potential traveling along an idealized straight and long axon is quadrupolar, meaning that it decays faster with distance than synaptic sources, which are typically dipolar (Nunez and Srinivasan, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about field potential physics, supported by citation.

claim: Synaptic sources are typically dipolar.
source: One of the reasons for the assumption that axonal currents contribute little to the EFP is that the far field of an action potential traveling along an idealized straight and long axon is quadrupolar, meaning that it decays faster with distance than synaptic sources, which are typically dipolar (Nunez and Srinivasan, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Theoretical and experimental studies indicated that the EFP of axonal responses may also have a dipolar structure.
source: Surprisingly, theoretical (Tenke et al., 1993) and experimental studies indicated that the EFP of axonal responses may also have a dipolar structure.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Blot and Barbour (2014) reported an EFP with a characteristic dipolar structure in the vicinity of cerebellar Purkinje cell axons.
source: For example, Blot and Barbour (2014) reported an EFP with a characteristic dipolar structure in the vicinity of cerebellar Purkinje cell axons
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: The axonal part of the EFP of thalamocortical afferents showed a polarity reversal associated with a dipolar source.
source: other studies (Swadlow et al., 2002; Swadlow and Gusev, 2000) showed that the axonal part of the EFP of thalamocortical afferents showed a polarity reversal associated with a dipolar source
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Classical current source density studies found dipolar current distributions in axonal terminal zones in the cortex and the lateral geniculate nucleus.
source: and classical current source density studies found dipolar current distributions in axonal terminal zones in the cortex and the lateral geniculate nucleus, and attributed these to axons because of conduction velocities (Mitzdorf and Singer, 1978; Mitzdorf, 1985; Mitzdorf and Singer, 1977; see also Tenke et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to classical studies.

claim: Dipolar current distributions in axonal terminal zones were attributed to axons because of conduction velocities.
source: and classical current source density studies found dipolar current distributions in axonal terminal zones in the cortex and the lateral geniculate nucleus, and attributed these to axons because of conduction velocities (Mitzdorf and Singer, 1978; Mitzdorf, 1985; Mitzdorf and Singer, 1977; see also Tenke et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to classical studies.

claim: The branchings and terminations of axons in their terminal zone area deform the extracellular waveform.
source: In particular, the branchings and terminations of axons in their terminal zone area deform the extracellular waveform (Gydikov et al., 1986; Gydikov and Trayanova, 1986; Plonsey, 1977) and can lead to a dipolar EFP structure.
evidence: This is supported by citations and is a key theoretical finding of the manuscript.

claim: Branchings and terminations of axons in their terminal zone can lead to a dipolar EFP structure.
source: In particular, the branchings and terminations of axons in their terminal zone area deform the extracellular waveform (Gydikov et al., 1986; Gydikov and Trayanova, 1986; Plonsey, 1977) and can lead to a dipolar EFP structure.
evidence: This is a key theoretical finding supported by modeling in the manuscript.

claim: Axon bundles exist throughout the peripheral and central nervous system and have terminal zones.
source: Axon bundles, sometimes called fascicles, exist throughout the peripheral and central nervous system and have such terminal zones (Kandel et al., 2000; Hentschel and van Ooyen, 1999; Nornes and Das, 1972; Goodman et al., 1984).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The white matter of the mammalian brain can be viewed as an agglomeration of fascicles.
source: The white matter of the mammalian brain can be viewed as an agglomeration of such fascicles (Schüz and Braitenberg, 2002).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Pronounced contributions of axon bundles to EFPs are neglected in current models.
source: We therefore predict pronounced contributions of axon bundles to EFPs, which are neglected in current models.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings and a critique of current modeling approaches.

claim: The extracellular action potential of a long axon approximating an infinitely long axon has a characteristic triphasic shape.
source: We began by simulating a long axon, approximating an infinitely long axon following a straight line path, neither bifurcating nor terminating (Figure 1A). The extracellular action potential has the characteristic triphasic shape.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: As the action potential travels along a long straight axon, the waveform is translated in time with the conduction velocity, but is otherwise unchanged.
source: As the action potential travels along the axon, the waveform is translated in time with the conduction velocity, but is otherwise unchanged.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data.

claim: The triphasic shape is present in the spatial arrangement of transmembrane currents at any given time.
source: The triphasic shape is also present in the spatial arrangement of transmembrane currents at any given time, which is the reason for the quadrupolar EFP response traditionally assumed for axons.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results and cable theory.

claim: The first small positive peak of the triphasic extracellular waveform corresponds to the capacitive current.
source: One way is by attribution of the peaks of the response to individual current types. The first, small positive peak corresponds to the capacitive current, the large and negative second peak to the sodium current, and the final positive peak to the potassium current (Gold et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The large and negative second peak of the triphasic extracellular waveform corresponds to the sodium current.
source: One way is by attribution of the peaks of the response to individual current types. The first, small positive peak corresponds to the capacitive current, the large and negative second peak to the sodium current, and the final positive peak to the potassium current (Gold et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The final positive peak of the triphasic extracellular waveform corresponds to the potassium current.
source: One way is by attribution of the peaks of the response to individual current types. The first, small positive peak corresponds to the capacitive current, the large and negative second peak to the sodium current, and the final positive peak to the potassium current (Gold et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The local transmembrane current in a homogeneous axon is proportional to the second spatial derivative of the membrane potential along the direction of the axon.
source: Due to Kirchhoff's law and cable theory (see Materials and methods), the local transmembrane current in a homogeneous axon is proportional to the second spatial derivative of the membrane potential along the direction of the axon.
evidence: This is derived from cable theory and Kirchhoff's law.

claim: When an action potential reaches a termination point, its EFP gradually deforms into a biphasic response, with a positive peak preceding a negative peak.
source: When the action potential reaches the termination point, its EFP gradually deforms into a biphasic response, with a positive peak preceding a negative peak.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The EFP near a bifurcation zone has a biphasic shape dominated by the second, negative and the third, positive peak.
source: The EFP near the bifurcation zone has a biphasic shape. Although there is an initial tiny positive peak, the response is dominated by the second, negative and the third, positive peak.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: An axon with bifurcations and terminations leads to biphasic responses at both the bifurcation and termination zones.
source: We found that this configuration leads to the same biphasic responses as observed in the cases of the isolated anatomical features.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The potential at the bifurcation and termination are both biphasic and on the same timescale, but opposite in polarity.
source: A notable point here is that the potential at the bifurcation and termination are both biphasic and on the same timescale, but opposite in polarity.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The summed extracellular population-level waveforms from axon bundles with randomized geometries showed a polarity reversal.
source: The resulting extracellular population-level waveforms (Figure 1E, right) showed a polarity reversal reminiscent of Figure 1D.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In the bifurcation zone, the summed contribution from many fibers and action potentials leads to a monophasic negative peak.
source: However, in the bifurcation zone, the summed contribution from many fibers and action potentials lead to a monophasic negative peak, and in the termination zone there was a monophasic positive peak.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In the termination zone, the summed contribution from many fibers and action potentials leads to a monophasic positive peak.
source: However, in the bifurcation zone, the summed contribution from many fibers and action potentials lead to a monophasic negative peak, and in the termination zone there was a monophasic positive peak.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The summed potential at the center of the terminal zone largely cancelled out.
source: Interestingly, the summed potential at the center of the terminal zone largely cancelled out.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Low-pass filtered EFP amplitudes showed a double-lobed shape typical of a dipole surrounding the terminal zone of the axon bundle.
source: Surrounding the terminal zone of the axon bundle in Figure 2A, low-pass filtered EFP amplitudes showed a double-lobed shape typical of a dipole.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The low-pass filtered EFP responses mostly showed monophasic deflections elicited by the population firing rate pulse.
source: In Figure 2B, the low-pass filtered EFP responses mostly showed monophasic deflections elicited by the population firing rate pulse, in a manner similar to that observed in Figure 1E.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The voltage deflection reverses polarity in the middle of the terminal zone of the bundle in the axial direction.
source: In the axial direction along the axon tree, i.e. in vertical direction in the figure, the voltage deflection reverses polarity in the middle of the terminal zone of the bundle (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The polarity reversal occurs by a decrease of the amplitude to zero and a subsequent reappearance with reversed polarity.
source: The polarity reversal occurs by a decrease of the amplitude to zero and a subsequent reappearance with reversed polarity (as opposed to a polarity reversal through a gradual shift in phase).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The point of the polarity reversal coincides with the middle of the terminal zone.
source: The point of the polarity reversal coincides with the middle of the terminal zone.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The absolute value of the response amplitude reaches a local minimum just at the axial location at which the number of axonal fibers reaches a maximum.
source: Interestingly, this means that the absolute value of the response amplitude reaches a local minimum just at the axial location at which the number of axonal fibers reaches a maximum.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The signed maximum amplitude EFP follows the distribution of branchings and terminations.
source: Overall, the signed maximum amplitude EFP (black trace) follows the distribution of branchings and terminations (purple histogram).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The iso-amplitude lines of the MUA appeared like an ellipsoid centered at the terminal zone.
source: In Figure 2D, the iso-amplitude lines of the MUA appeared like an ellipsoid centered at the terminal zone (Figure 2D); they did not show the double-lobe shape observed for the low-pass filtered EFP in Figure 2A.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The amplitude of the MUA component changes in accordance with the local number of nodes per unit length.
source: The amplitude of the MUA component (black trace) changes in accordance with the local number of nodes per unit length (teal-colored histogram), which is proportional to the number of fibers.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: At low frequencies (<1 kHz), the response of the bifurcating case exceeded the control by a factor 20 at distances larger than 1 mm.
source: Interestingly, for distances larger than 1 mm the response in the bifurcating case exceeded the control by a factor 20.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At low frequencies, the bifurcation zone contributes supralinearly to the dipole moment.
source: We thus concluded that at low frequencies, the bifurcation zone contributes supralinearly to the dipole moment.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The presence of a bifurcation zone did not contribute to the high-frequency dipole moments in the EFP.
source: Thus, the presence of a bifurcation zone did not contribute to the high-frequency dipole moments in the EFP.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The dipole moment of the bifurcating case has a maximum at around 500 Hz.
source: The dipole moment of the bifurcating case (solid line) has a maximum at around 500 Hz, as expected due to the agreement of the spatial wavelength (1 m/s / 500 Hz = 2 mm; gray vertical line in Figure 3D and C) and axial width (about 2 mm; gray box in Figure 3A and B) of the projection zone.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The contribution of the terminal zone is greater than 10 for intermediate frequencies between about 200 and 1300 Hz.
source: The contribution of the terminal zone is greater than 10 (dotted line) for intermediate frequencies between about 200 and 1300 Hz, and smaller than a factor 10 outside this frequency range.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The barn owl has a highly developed auditory system with a strong frequency-following response in the EFP up to 9 kHz.
source: The barn owl has a highly developed auditory system with a strong frequency-following response in the EFP (up to 9 kHz, [Köppl, 1997b]), called the neurophonic, which can be recorded in the nucleus laminaris (NL).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The EFP in nucleus laminaris is mainly due to the afferent activity.
source: The EFP in this region is mainly due to the afferent activity, and the contribution of postsynaptic NL spikes is small (Kuokkanen et al., 2010; Kuokkanen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The contribution of postsynaptic NL spikes to the EFP is small.
source: The EFP in this region is mainly due to the afferent activity, and the contribution of postsynaptic NL spikes is small (Kuokkanen et al., 2010; Kuokkanen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Two fiber bundles enter the nucleus laminaris, with fibers from the contralateral ear entering ventrally, and from the ipsilateral ear entering dorsally.
source: Furthermore, the anatomy of the afferent axons is well known and follows a stereotypical pattern (Carr and Konishi, 1988; Carr and Konishi, 1990): Two fiber bundles enter the nucleus, with fibers from the contralateral ear entering ventrally, and from the ipsilateral ear entering dorsally.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The axon bundles reach the NL from their origin without bifurcating, then bifurcate multiple times at the border of the NL, and then terminate within NL.
source: The axon bundles reach the NL from their origin without bifurcating, then bifurcate multiple times at the border of the NL, and then terminate within NL.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Most of the volume within NL consists of incoming axons.
source: Most of the volume within NL consists of incoming axons.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The click responses showed distinct low-frequency and high-frequency components.
source: The click responses showed distinct low-frequency (Figure 4B) and high-frequency (Figure 4C) components, as previously reported (Wagner et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and citation to previous work.

claim: The frequency of the high-frequency ringing corresponds to the recording location on the frequency map within NL.
source: The frequency of the high-frequency ringing corresponds to the recording location on the frequency map within NL, and the ringing reflects the frequency tuning and phase locking of the incoming axons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NL physiology.

claim: The high-frequency ringing reflects the frequency tuning and phase locking of the incoming axons.
source: The frequency of the high-frequency ringing corresponds to the recording location on the frequency map within NL, and the ringing reflects the frequency tuning and phase locking of the incoming axons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NL physiology.

claim: The inferred number of fibers has its maximum at the center of the electrode array, and decays steadily to both sides.
source: The number (scaled by an arbitrary factor) has its maximum at the center of the electrode array, and decays steadily to both sides.
evidence: This is supported by model fitting to experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The profile of the number of fibers inferred from model fitting is consistent with the known anatomy of axons in NL.
source: This profile of the number of fibers is consistent with the known anatomy of axons in NL (Carr and Konishi, 1990; Kuokkanen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of model results with anatomical knowledge from citations.

claim: The low-frequency responses at the dorsal and ventral edges show the same shape, but with opposite polarity, as expected for a dipolar field.
source: The low-frequency responses at the dorsal and ventral edges in Figure 5C show the same shape, but with opposite polarity, as expected for a dipolar field.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The axonal conduction velocity in NL was calculated to be 4.0 m/s.
source: The axonal conduction velocity was calculated to be 4.0 m/s, and the distance from the bundle was 162 µm.
evidence: This is derived from model fitting to experimental data.

claim: A previously published estimate of the axonal conduction velocity in nucleus laminaris gave a confidence bound of 0.4–6 m/s.
source: A previously published estimate of the axonal conduction velocity in this nucleus (McColgan et al., 2014) gave a confidence bound of 0.4–6 m/s.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Using the derived formula, the predicted contribution to the ABR from an axon bundle in NL was 3.1 µV at 2 cm distance.
source: We calculated the contribution expected from an axon bundle with the same characteristics as described before at 2 cm from NL, aiming to estimate the contribution to the ABR. Multiplying by a factor of 2 to account for the fact that there is an NL in each hemisphere, the predicted contribution was 3.1 µV, which is of the same order of magnitude as the value reported in the experiments.
evidence: This is calculated using the analytical model (Equation 1) with parameters from barn owl NL.

claim: An amplitude of about 10 µV of the ABR in the barn owl has been reported by Palanca-Castan et al. (2016).
source: An amplitude of about 10 µV of the ABR in the barn owl has recently been reported by Palanca-Castan et al. (2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The predicted contribution of 3.1 µV is of the same order of magnitude as the value reported in the experiments for the ABR.
source: Multiplying by a factor of 2 to account for the fact that there is an NL in each hemisphere, the predicted contribution was 3.1 µV, which is of the same order of magnitude as the value reported in the experiments.
evidence: This is an inference comparing the model prediction with experimental data.

claim: Synaptic contributions to the EFP in NL are expected to be small because somatic membrane potentials due to synaptic currents are much smaller than the impact of postsynaptic spikes.
source: We believe synaptic contributions to be small in this case for the following reasons: The somatic membrane potentials due to synaptic currents are much smaller than the impact of postsynaptic spikes (Ashida et al., 2007; Funabiki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited physiological data.

claim: Synaptic sources cannot explain a dipolar EFP in NL because of the symmetrical arrangement of synapses on the spherical NL cell bodies.
source: Furthermore, synaptic EFP contributions would require a spatial separation of currents, which is not possible to achieve in NL because of the symmetrical arrangement of synapses on the spherical NL cell bodies (Carr and Konishi, 1990), meaning that synaptic sources can also not explain a dipolar EFP, and are thus expected to contribute little to the EFP.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A similar dipole-like reversal of polarity has been reported in the chicken NL.
source: It is interesting to note that a similar dipole-like reversal of polarity as shown here for the barn owl NL has been reported in the chicken NL (Schwarz, 1992)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A similar dipole-like reversal of polarity has been reported in the mammalian medial superior olive (MSO).
source: It is interesting to note that a similar dipole-like reversal of polarity as shown here for the barn owl NL has been reported in the chicken NL (Schwarz, 1992) as well as in the mammalian analog to NL, the medial superior olive (MSO) (Mc Laughlin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The phase reversal in chicken NL and mammalian MSO was modeled based on the assumption that the postsynaptic dendrites with their bipolar morphology generate the dipolar EFP response.
source: The phase reversal in this case was modeled based on the assumption that the postsynaptic NL and MSO dendrites with their bipolar morphology generate the dipolar EFP response (Mc Laughlin et al., 2010; Goldwyn et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: In the barn owl, the bipolar morphology of neurons is largely absent.
source: However, in the owl this dipolar morphology of neurons is largely absent (Carr and Konishi, 1990), making dendritic sources unlikely.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Similar dipolar field potentials in owls and mammals emerge from different physiological substrates.
source: This differential morphology suggests that similar dipolar field potentials in owls and mammals emerge from different physiological substrates.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical differences.

claim: The degree of direction in the growth of an axon depends on the balance struck between conduction delay and wiring cost.
source: Cuntz et al. (2010) and Budd et al. (2010) studied the principles underlying the growth patterns of axons and found that the degree of direction in the growth of an axon depends on the balance struck between conduction delay and wiring cost.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Optimizing for minimal conduction time leads to highly directed axonal structures.
source: Optimizing for minimal conduction time leads to highly directed structures while optimizing wiring cost leads to more tortuous, undirected growth.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on axonal growth.

claim: Optimizing wiring cost leads to more tortuous, undirected axonal growth.
source: Optimizing for minimal conduction time leads to highly directed structures while optimizing wiring cost leads to more tortuous, undirected growth.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on axonal growth.

claim: Directed axonal structures and strong, dipolar EFPs due to axons may be more prevalent in systems which require high temporal precision in the information processing.
source: This insight suggests that directed structures - and thus also strong, dipolar EFPs due to axons - may be more prevalent in systems which require high temporal precision in the information processing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between axonal structure and function.

claim: The dipole moment is maximal when the spatial spread of the activation is equal to the size of the projection zone.
source: This requirement for high temporal precision also aligns well with our model prediction: the dipole moment (Equation 1) is maximal when the spatial spread of the activation is equal to the size of the projection zone, favoring short activation times (<1 ms) for typical projection zone sizes (1 mm) and conduction velocities (1 m/s).
evidence: This is derived from the analytical model (Equation 1).

claim: Axonal contributions might be relevant in the analysis of EEG fields.
source: As originally suggested by Tenke et al. (1993), we propose that axonal contributions might also be relevant in the analysis of these fields.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings and supported by citation.

claim: Axonal contributions are particularly relevant for the auditory brainstem response (ABR).
source: This is particularly true for the auditory brainstem response (ABR), which is closely related to the EEG and involves brain structures that display high degrees of synchrony as well as axonal organization, and are thus ideal candidates for the generation of axonal field potentials visible at long ranges.
evidence: This is an inference based on the characteristics of the ABR and the findings of the study.

claim: In the case of axon fiber bundles, the number of fibers is variable in space, particularly in the terminal zone.
source: In contrast, in the case of axon fiber bundles, the situation is different: the number of fibers is variable in space, in particular in the terminal zone, but the current sources at different locations are highly correlated because they are caused by propagating action potentials.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of axon bundles.

claim: In axon fiber bundles, the current sources at different locations are highly correlated because they are caused by propagating action potentials.
source: In contrast, in the case of axon fiber bundles, the situation is different: the number of fibers is variable in space, in particular in the terminal zone, but the current sources at different locations are highly correlated because they are caused by propagating action potentials.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of axon bundles.

claim: It was possible to recover the normalized fiber densities and average membrane potentials from the recordings in the case where axonal action potentials dominate the EFP.
source: In the case presented here (Figure 5) where axonal action potentials dominate the EFP, it was possible to recover the (normalized) fiber densities and average membrane potentials from the recordings.
evidence: This is supported by the model fitting results shown in Figure 5.
